title: Your Backpack Pocket Full of Pesos Is a Clue: Argentina Spending, Decoded
summary: Inflation, three exchange rates, and a QR code on every counter. How a digital nomad actually handles everyday spending in Argentina in 2026, from cafes to colectivos.
body_markdown:
Saturday morning at the Feria de San Telmo. You hand over a stack of thousand peso notes for a leather belt and the vendor counts them twice, folds them into a brick the size of a sandwich, and tucks it under the table with all the ceremony of someone filing paperwork. Then the woman behind you steps up, points her phone at a laminated QR code taped to the table leg, taps twice, and walks off with a mate gourd. Total elapsed time: maybe eight seconds. You, meanwhile, are still re-zipping the pocket where you keep your cash brick.


That little scene is Argentina's money situation in miniature. Cash still works everywhere, but inflation has turned it into a volume problem, and locals have quietly moved an enormous share of daily life onto QR codes. Here is how to keep up.


## Why everyone's wallet looks like a deck of cards


Years of inflation mean prices carry a lot of zeros, and the physical notes have not kept pace. So a normal day of spending (coffee, lunch, a SUBE top-up, groceries, maybe a taxi) can involve a genuinely thick stack of bills. Argentines have adapted with rubber bands, money clips, and a casual fluency in counting notes at speed that visitors find slightly intimidating.


They have also adapted by scanning. Mercado Pago, the payments arm of Mercado Libre, is close to universal: the little blue QR stand sits on the counter of kiosks, verdulerías, parrillas, pharmacies, and the guy selling churros outside the Subte. MODO, backed by the country's banks, is the other half of the ecosystem, and the QR codes are broadly interoperable, which means one printed code on the counter serves almost everyone. If you are wondering how to pay in Argentina day to day, the honest answer is that locals mostly point their phones at that code.


## The three prices of a dollar, briefly


Here is the part that melts visitors' brains. Argentina has lived with more than one exchange rate for years. There is an official rate, there are market rates people talk about over dinner, and there is the rate your foreign card applies, which has shifted around as policies change. Ask three expats which rate you should be getting and you will hear three confident, contradictory answers, all of which were true at some point.


You do not need to become an economist. You need one habit: never agree to pay in your home currency, and always know what rate you are getting before money moves. The rate landscape changes, but that rule does not. It is also the core reason a transparent wallet beats guessing. When you pay through Moreta Pay, the app shows you the amount in pesos, the FX rate, and the merchant's name on screen before you confirm, so the question of "wait, which rate did I just get?" is answered before you tap, not on a statement three days later.


## Joining the scan economy without an Argentine bank account


Here is where visitors usually hit a wall. Mercado Pago and MODO are built around local identity documents and local bank accounts. As a nomad or a new expat, you typically cannot just download them and start scanning, which is frustrating when the entire city is paying that way around you.


Moreta Pay exists precisely for this gap. You top up the wallet from home (a US bank via Plaid or ACH, SEPA from Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card), keep the balance in your own currency, and then scan the same QR codes locals use. Point your camera at the code on the empanada counter, check the peso amount and the rate, confirm, and the merchant is paid instantly in pesos. No local account, no cash brick, no mental arithmetic about which rate you are eating. If you have already used it elsewhere in the region, say for

## A phone-first day in Buenos Aires


What does Argentina without cash actually look like in practice? Something like this:


**Morning:**


cortado and medialunas at a cafe in Palermo. QR stand on the counter, scan, confirm, done.


**Midday:**


lunch at a menú del día spot in Microcentro. Same move.


**Afternoon:**


groceries at a chino (the neighborhood supermarket), pharmacy run, maybe a coworking day pass. All QR.


**Evening:**


parrilla with friends, where splitting the bill is easier when everyone can see exact amounts instead of dividing a pile of notes by five.


Online is covered too. Booking a side trip to Mendoza or a hotel in Bariloche through platforms that accept QR-based checkout works the same way: scan, review, confirm. The one thing you will still want pesos for is the SUBE transit card and the odd vendor who is purely cash, which brings us to the last point.


## Keep a thin stack, not a brick


Some cash is still smart in Argentina. Street fairs, small-town stops, tips, bus fare, the occasional vendor who offers a discount for efectivo. The goal is not zero cash, it is carrying a thin, boring amount instead of a brick, and replacing ATM runs with scans wherever possible.


That matters because ATMs in Argentina combine low withdrawal limits with the classic double-fee squeeze, where your bank charges you on one end and the machine operator charges you on the other. We broke down exactly


[why ATMs charge you twice](https://moretapay.com/blog/why-atm-networks-charge-you-twice-unpacking-the-issuing-bank-fee)


in a separate piece, but the short version is that frequent small withdrawals are the most expensive possible way to fund a trip here. Every purchase you shift onto a QR code is one fewer withdrawal, one fewer queue, and one fewer moment of counting notes in public while a line forms behind you.


## The shape of a good Argentina setup


Put it all together and the setup is simple. Land with a modest amount of pesos for transit and edge cases. Do everything else by scanning the Mercado Pago and MODO codes that are already on every counter, with Moreta Pay as your way into that system since the local apps will not enroll you. Check the rate on screen each time you pay, enjoy the small smugness of skipping the ATM line, and save your pocket space for actual souvenirs instead of rubber-banded currency.
